title: Accessible names and descriptions
learningObjectives: Explain accessible names and descriptions and apply inclusive semantic HTML practices.

understand.concept: An accessible name identifies a control or element, while an accessible description provides additional information. Names may come from visible labels, associated label elements, aria-labelledby, or aria-label where appropriate. Descriptions can be connected with aria-describedby.
understand.whyItMatters: Users of assistive technology need to identify controls and understand instructions or errors. Prefer visible labels and avoid using placeholder text as the only name.
understand.analogy: The accessible name is the control's name tag; the description is the extra note that explains how to use it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; accessibility APIs, semantics, and assistive technology behaviour require standards-based implementation and testing.

explain.narrative: The label provides the input's accessible name, while aria-describedby connects the supporting text as its description.

examples.code: <form><label for='email'>Email address</label><input id='email' type='email' aria-describedby='email-help'><small id='email-help'>We will use this for course updates.</small></form>
examples.explanation: The label provides the input's accessible name, while aria-describedby connects the supporting text as its description.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered semantic HTML example demonstrating the accessibility principle.

practise.guidedTask: Create a form with visible labels and descriptions. Inspect the accessibility tree and test the control with a screen reader where available.
practise.independentTask: Audit a small page using keyboard navigation and an accessibility tree. Fix semantics, labels, alternatives, and relationships without adding unnecessary ARIA.
hints: Use native HTML where it provides the required semantics.
Keep visible labels and focus indicators.
Test meaningful content with keyboard and assistive technology where available.

practice.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Accessible names and descriptions</title></head><body>
<form><label for='email'>Email address</label><input id='email' type='email' aria-describedby='email-help'><small id='email-help'>We will use this for course updates.</small></form>
</body></html>
practice.resetCode:

<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Accessible names and descriptions</title></head><body>

questions.prompt: Which attribute commonly connects supporting instructions to a control?
questions.explanation: aria-describedby references text that provides an accessible description.

questions.prompt: What is a good accessibility workflow?
options: Use semantic HTML first, then add only necessary ARIA and test
Add ARIA roles to every element
questions.answer: Use semantic HTML first, then add only necessary ARIA and test
questions.explanation: Native semantics provide a strong baseline and testing reveals real interaction barriers.
